title: Hamstrings
source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 11.6 Appendicular Muscles of the Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs; 11.1; 13.4

main.t: The three long muscles at the back of the thigh that bend the knee and extend the hip.

simpler.t: The hamstrings are the muscles at the back of your thigh. They bend your knee.

deeper.t: They are the biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus, in the posterior compartment of the thigh.

facts.t: The hamstrings fill the posterior compartment of the thigh.
All three arise from the ischial tuberosity; the biceps femoris also from the linea aspera and distal femur.

simpler.t: They run from the bone you sit on to the back of the knee.

deeper.t: Their tendons form the borders of the popliteal fossa, the diamond-shaped space behind the knee.

items.name: Biceps femoris
items.t: The lateral hamstring. Besides flexing the knee, it turns the thigh outwards.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). Which hamstrings lie laterally and which medially (OpenStax gives their rotations, not their positions).

items.name: Semitendinosus
items.t: A medial hamstring with a long tendon. It turns the thigh inwards.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The long tendon of the semitendinosus, and which hamstrings lie medially.

items.name: Semimembranosus
items.t: A medial hamstring, deep to the semitendinosus. It turns the thigh inwards.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). That the semimembranosus lies deep to the semitendinosus, and which hamstrings lie medially.

items.name: Popliteal fossa
items.t: The diamond-shaped space behind the knee, bordered by their tendons.

simpler.t: One hamstring is on the outer side; two are on the inner side.
simpler.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). Which hamstrings lie laterally and which medially (OpenStax gives their rotations, not their positions).

deeper.t: The biceps femoris inserts on the head of the fibula; the other two on the medial side of the tibia.
deeper.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The insertions of the hamstrings.

facts.t: Crossing the back of the knee, they flex the leg, as when kneeling.
Crossing the back of the hip, they also extend the thigh: they move it down and back.
They oppose the quadriceps, which extend the knee.

simpler.t: They bend the knee and swing the thigh backwards.

items.name: Ischial tuberosity
items.t: Their common origin, on the hip bone.

items.name: Sciatic nerve
items.t: Runs down the back of the thigh. It is the tibial and fibular nerves combined.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). That the sciatic nerve supplies the hamstrings and runs among them.

items.name: Gastrocnemius
items.t: Arises from the femoral condyles, so it too crosses the back of the knee and helps flex it.

items.name: Gracilis
items.t: In the medial compartment. Like the hamstrings, it moves the leg back at the knee, as when kneeling.

simpler.t: They sit behind the thigh, opposite the quadriceps, with the sciatic nerve close by.

facts.t: Like all limb muscles, they develop from general mesoderm, and each fibre forms from many fused myoblasts.
Sprinters’ muscles have a high share of fast glycolytic fibres for powerful bursts.
facts.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). Fibre types of the hamstrings specifically.

items.injury: A sudden sprint, with the hip flexed and the knee straightening.
items.damaged: The hamstrings, which tear (a hamstring strain).
items.cannotDo: Run or bend the knee against resistance without pain.
items.why: They are stretched across two joints while contracting hard to slow the leg.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). Hamstring strains.

items.injury: Compression of the sciatic nerve or the spinal nerves that form it.
items.cannotDo: Move the hip and leg without pain.
items.why: Compression or irritation of the nerve, or of the spinal nerves forming it, causes sciatica.

items.q: Explain why the hamstrings act on both the hip and the knee.
model: They arise from the ischial tuberosity, behind the hip joint.
They cross the back of the knee to the leg.
So they extend the thigh at the hip.
And they flex the leg at the knee.

items.q: Compare the biceps femoris with the semitendinosus and semimembranosus.
model: All three flex the knee and extend the thigh.
The biceps femoris lies laterally and turns the thigh outwards.
The other two lie medially and turn it inwards.
Only the biceps femoris also arises from the femur.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). Which hamstrings lie laterally and which medially (OpenStax gives their rotations, not their positions).

items.q: Predict which movement is hard after a hamstring strain.
model: Swinging the thigh back while running.
Both stretch or load the torn muscle.
So running and climbing hurt most.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). Hamstring strains.

check.stem: Where do all three hamstrings arise?
check.why: All three arise from the ischial tuberosity.

check.stem: What space do the hamstring tendons help to form?
check.why: Their tendons form the popliteal fossa behind the knee.

check.stem: Which hamstring turns the thigh outwards?
check.why: The biceps femoris twists the thigh outwards; the other two twist it inwards.
